items.abstract: Abstract Despite growing acceptance of the importance of groundwater use by hominins, there has been little hydrogeological investigation into the controls on groundwater availability as relevant to their evolution and geographic dispersal. This study integrates available fossil and stone tool data with hydrogeological landscape reconstruction and conceptualisation to develop understanding and constraints on the earliest use of groundwater by hominins and early migrations between Africa and Eurasia. It is proposed that the first bipedal human ancestors, appearing in the fossil record in Central and East Africa between 6 and 7 Ma, learned from other mammals how to find and access shallow groundwater in ephemeral streambeds. The first evidence of hominin associations with groundwater discharge from springs is from around 2–4.5 Ma in the East African Rift System (EARS), these locations likely being critically stable hydro-refugia within the driest parts of precession-dominated climatic cycles. The first migrating hominin species appears to have been Homo erectus , with those in the EARS leaving in waves as small bands from around 1.9 Ma at the end of a humid period in the Arabian Peninsula. It is proposed that the most hydrologically plausible routes linking the EARS to Eurasia are via Red Sea crossings and then through the Arabian Peninsula moving along the strike of regional aquifers which would have provided perennial groundwater even over long climatically arid periods. The paper demonstrates the fundamental importance of groundwater for early hominin communities during a critical period in the evolution of human physiology and consciousness.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The physical effects of interpersonal violence are well documented in archaeology, but its broader impacts on population health, mobility, and resource access remain less understood. This article assesses how chronic warfare restricted movement and access to critical resources, altering dietary practices and contributing to persistent food insecurity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We develop a replicable framework for using coupled biological and isotopic data to evaluate elevated δ
                      <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                      N values in archaeological populations. The framework is applied to the Nazca highlands of Peru during the Late Intermediate Period (LIP; 1000–1450 
                      <jats:sc>ce</jats:sc>
                      ), a context marked by persistent violence and regional instability. We analyze δ
                      <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                      N, δ
                      <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                      C, and δ
                      <jats:sup>34</jats:sup>
                      S data from 149 radiocarbon‐dated individuals alongside osteological evidence, paleoclimatic proxies, and dietary baselines.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Nazca highland LIP individuals exhibit elevated δ
                      <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                      N values (mean = 13.36‰). Carbon isotopes indicate reliance on C4 resources (mean δ
                      <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                      Ccollagen = −10.38‰; mean δ
                      <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                      Ccarbonate = −6.98‰), while δ
                      <jats:sup>34</jats:sup>
                      S values are low (mean≈4.1‰). Elevated δ
                      <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                      N did not vary by age or sex, while LIP individuals exhibited greater skeletal stress and extensive interpersonal violence.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Persistent conflict and restricted mobility altered Nazca highland food production and access. Dependence on land near fortified settlements may have encouraged intensive cultivation and camelid dung fertilization, raising dietary δ
                      <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                      N. Reduced mobility also constrained strategies for buffering seasonal shortfalls, increasing recurrent food insecurity and catabolism that may have further enriched human δ
                      <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                      N. Consistently elevated nitrogen values therefore reflect subsistence changes associated with sustained warfare and constrained access to land and resources.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
authors: Sarah J. Noe, Bridgette Degnan, Emily C. Kracht, Weston C. McCool

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Maximum gape and bite force are two key metrics of primate craniodental performance, but without mitigating adaptations, large gapes are associated with reduced bite force. Primate craniodental morphology undergoes functional transitions across development, but how these performance variables vary with life‐history transitions is unknown.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Maximum gapes of 211 rhesus macaques (
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                        <jats:italic>Macaca mulatta</jats:italic>
                      </jats:styled-content>
                      ) spanning infancy to post‐prime developmental stages from Cayo Santiago (Puerto Rico) were collected in vivo, and jaw leverage, a contributor to bite force, was calculated from skeletal measurements of the same individuals post‐mortem. Allometric relationships were tested using a combination of OLS regressions and mixed‐effects models with developmental stage and sex as interaction terms.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In vivo gape did not differ from isometry relative to body mass and jaw length across developmental stages by sex, but jaw leverage was significantly lower in larger compared to smaller macaques. The largest developmental differences occurred between pre‐prime and prime individuals. Canine length scaled with positive allometry against body mass and jaw length in males but not females, while maximum gape scaled with negative allometry relative to canine length in both sexes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These results indicate that macaques undergo a functional tradeoff between jaw leverage and gape around the onset of sexual dimorphism. Pre‐prime macaques exhibit relatively greater jaw leverage, whereas adults maintain proportionate gape relative to body and jaw size at reduced mechanical advantage. The eruption of large canines in males does not influence linear gape outside of size differences captured by body mass and jaw length.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
authors: Stephanie L. Canington, Cassandra M. Turcotte, Eva M. Hernandez‐Janer, Michala K. Stock, Catalina I. Villamil, Cayo Biobank Research Unit, Michael J. Montague, Melween I. Martinez, Scott A. Williams, Susan C. Antón, James P. Higham, Myra F. Laird

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Primates have adaptations that mitigate the functional consequences of dental wear. One such adaptation is dentin deposition within the pulp chamber, which may extend tooth functionality. Because this deposition can reflect age‐related secondary dentin and stimulus‐driven tertiary dentin, it remains unclear whether the resulting pulp volume reduction primarily tracks cumulative wear, chronological age, or aspects of occlusal morphology. Here, we test covariation among pulp chamber volume, dental wear, and dental topography in captive baboons. MicroCT and occlusal scans were used to evaluate relationships among pulp volume, dental wear, and dental topography for
                    <jats:italic>M</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                    –
                    <jats:italic>M</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    from 46 adult baboons that were part of the Southwest National Primate Research Center. Ages of death were adjusted for molar eruption timing to calculate “wear age,” representing the duration each tooth was in occlusion. Wear age was positively correlated with dental wear metrics and showed weaker relationships with dental topography. Corrected pulp volume was negatively associated with wear age, dentin exposure ratio, and Krueger‐Scott scores, while relief index (RFI) was the only dental‐topography measure associated with pulp volume across molars. These results suggest that pulp chamber reduction in baboons reflects both cumulative wear and the functional effects of occlusal morphology. Because RFI in worn teeth reflects wear‐related changes in crown geometry, we hypothesize that variation in occlusal relief may also relate to differences in how mechanical loads are distributed across the crown. These proposed relationships remain to be tested directly. Patterns of pulp chamber remodeling may therefore vary across taxa with dental morphology and loading environment.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Myra F. Laird, Diego A. Contreras, Leslea J. Hlusko, Kristin L. Krueger

items.abstract: Abstract This study proposes an automated method for detecting tooth positions and predicting full-mouth series (FMS) radiograph placement using oriented object detection and Siamese neural networks. A total of 5,431 radiographs from 354 patients were annotated and used to train deep learning models. Oriented bounding boxes were generated using a YOLOv5 detector, followed by tooth numbering, feature extraction, and image classification via a multitask ResNet50 model. FMS placement was predicted using a Siamese neural network inspired by jigsaw-puzzle tasks, with permutation-based training and patient-level five-fold cross-validation. Mean tooth-numbering accuracy was 0.99 ± 0.00. Mean FMS-placement accuracy was 0.97 ± 0.01 for upper left and right periapical radiographs, 0.98 ± 0.02 for upper anterior periapical radiographs, 0.98 ± 0.01 for lower left and right periapical radiographs, 0.99 ± 0.01 for lower anterior periapical radiographs, and 0.96 ± 0.02 for bitewing radiographs; overall mean accuracy was 0.98 ± 0.01. This internally tested AI pipeline demonstrated high accuracy for tooth numbering and automated FMS arrangement and may help streamline dental radiographic workflows, subject to external and clinical validation.
